displayQuote: Sports do not build character. They reveal it

meta.title: Who really said "Sports do not build character. They reveal it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not John Wooden. The saying traces to CBS sportscaster Heywood Hale Broun in the early 1970s, polished into its famous form in Michener's Sports in America (1976).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Sports do not build character. They reveal it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not John Wooden. It's Heywood Hale Broun, via 1974 speeches and the 1976 book Sports in America. The Wooden credit only surfaces in 2006.

answer.label: Not John Wooden — actually Heywood Hale Broun
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Broun’s, from talks he gave in the early-to-mid 1970s — but he said it in looser words (“Sports reveals character, it doesn’t build it”). The polished line everyone quotes was set down in James A. Michener’s Sports in America (1976), credited there to Broun. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the John Wooden credit only from 2006 onward and rates the evidence for it weak.
answer.confidenceText: Origin traced to Heywood Hale Broun; the famous wording is a 1976 streamlining, not John Wooden.

source.excerpt: Sports do not build character. They reveal it.
trail: January 1974 — Ames Daily Tribune (Iowa). The earliest strong match logged by Quote Investigator ↗, reporting Broun: “But sport doesn’t build character… Sports reveals character.”
May 1974 — The Salina Journal (Kansas). Two reports of Broun on the lecture circuit, including “Sports reveals character, it doesn’t build it,” per QI’s citation list ↗.

1976 — Michener, Sports in America, p. 16. The concise modern wording, credited to Broun; the p. 16 page reference is Quote Investigator’s, against the 1976 Random House first edition. A later edition is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗, so its pagination need not match.
2006 — Hood County News (Granbury, Texas). The first Wooden ascription QI records, thirty-odd years downstream and unsupported by anything earlier — see the investigation ↗.
source.excerptNote: The words as Broun was actually reported saying them in 1974 were looser: “But sport doesn’t build character… Sports reveals character,” and, at a Kansas lecture that May, “Sports reveals character, it doesn’t build it.”

author.name: Heywood Hale Broun
author.heading: About Heywood Hale Broun
author.bio: Heywood Hale Broun — son of the columnist Heywood Broun and the feminist Ruth Hale — wrote for PM and the New York Star before CBS hired him in 1966 as a roving sports essayist. For roughly two decades, in loud jackets and a “merry mustache,” he filed Saturday-night features on everything from Super Bowls to county-fair oddities. He was a skeptic of sport’s moral claims, arguing repeatedly in 1970s lectures that character is formed long before the whistle blows.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit — and who should
misattribution.intro: Three different names circulate on this one, and only one of them has 1970s paper behind this wording.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Wooden ascription only in 2006, in the Hood County News of Granbury, Texas, decades after the saying was in circulation, and calls the supporting evidence weak. What a 1996 article actually attributed to Wooden was the opposite-leaning “Yes, sports can build character. But they also can tear down character.”

Quote sites routinely file the line under the elder Heywood Broun, the New York World columnist, rather than his son. The sportscaster who actually said it is Heywood Hale Broun ↗, born 1918 — his father died in 1939, long before the 1970s citations.

items.scope: A near neighbour, not the same line
items.why: The Texas coach’s 1975 variant — football doesn’t build character, it eliminates the weak ones — is collected alongside this one in Barry Popik’s file ↗, and is sometimes conflated with it.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit the idea to Heywood Hale Broun, who argued it in speeches documented from 1971 — but note that the crisp two-sentence wording everyone shares was likely streamlined in James A. Michener’s 1976 book ↗, not spoken that way by Broun.

context.heading: Why the line stuck — and why it drifted to Wooden
lead: The 1970s were a bad decade for the belief that games make you good. A widely reported 1971 psychological study of athletes punctured the idea that sport forges virtue, and Broun — a professional watcher of athletes at close range — kept making the same point on the lecture circuit: character is largely set by the age of six or seven, and the field merely turns the lights on it.

Coaches, though, are the people who get quoted about character, and John Wooden is the most quotable coach America has produced. A line that sounds like sideline wisdom migrates naturally toward the man with the pyramid of success, even though what Wooden was actually recorded saying in the 1990s was more equivocal — that sport can build character, and can tear it down too.
detailsBody: The tidiest version of the saying — two short sentences, a pivot on “reveal” — is the one in Michener’s Sports in America. Quote Investigator’s reading is that Michener, or his source, streamlined Broun’s spoken remarks into their memorable shape, which is how most aphorisms actually reach us.
context.pull: Character is built pretty much by the time you’re six or seven. Sports reveals character.
